The control stays a native password field, so password managers, autofill and form submission work as they do everywhere else. Put form options like `name`, `required` and `autoComplete` on `PasswordInput`, and input attributes like `id` and `placeholder` on `PasswordInputControl`.
The score, from 0 for empty to 4.

The toggle is a toggle button with a fixed name, “Show password”, and `aria-pressed` tells screen readers whether the password is shown. Rename it for other secrets and languages. A pointer press on the toggle keeps the caret where it was in the field.
The toggle sits on the left, and the strength meter fills from the right. Pass labels in your language.

`PasswordInputCapsLock` opens below the field while Caps Lock is on and the field has focus, and says so through a status region. `PasswordInputStrength` is a meter whose value text is the strength label, read on demand rather than announced on every key. Shown passwords skip spellcheck, autocorrect and capitalization.

`PasswordInputStrength` scores the password from 0 to 4 as it’s typed. The checklist reads the same value with `usePasswordInputValue()`. The rules belong to the example, since the component sets no password policy.

`autoComplete` defaults to `current-password` for signing in. Use `new-password` to sign up or change a password, so the browser offers a strong one, and `off` for secrets that aren’t account passwords.
`defaultVisible` starts with the text showing, for a secret people need to read, like a Wi-Fi password.
`invalid` marks the field and sets `aria-invalid` on the input. Point its `aria-describedby` at your message. A required field also turns red after someone leaves it empty.
